fields.Front: What are the 'rules of the game' for representing relationships with only tables?
fields.Back:
1. You may add as many new COLUMNS and ROWS as you want to the existing tables
2. If you need a new TABLE you may add that too
3. That is ALL you may add or delete - columns, rows and tables. No pointers, no nested records, no lists in cells.

fields.Front: Why does the foreign key go on the N side of a 1:N relationship, and what wrong idea does the instructor try first?
fields.Back: Each N-side row relates to AT MOST ONE 1-side row, so a single cell suffices. The wrong idea: an extra column in DEPARTMENT holding 'Laura's ID, Doug's ID and Jamie's ID with commas in between them' - it fails first normal form, because cells must hold one value. Computer Science has three professors, so the reverse direction would need a list.

fields.Front: PROFESSOR (M) Works for (1) DEPARTMENT, with relationship attributes Hours and StartDate. What changes, and which new columns are foreign keys?
fields.Back: PROFESSOR gains DeptID (FK), Hours and StartDate; DEPARTMENT is unchanged. ONLY DeptID is a foreign key - 'Hours and StartDate are not foreign keys, because they're not actually keys; they're just attributes on the relationship'. PROFESSOR's primary key is still EmpID; DEPARTMENT has primary key DeptID and no foreign keys yet.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: use the professor and department tables to answer 'which building does Laura Reid work in?'
fields.Back: Laura's DeptID is CS; go to DEPARTMENT, look up CS, which is Computer Science in Middlesex College. 'You use the keys to answer different queries' - following a foreign key to the matching primary key is exactly what a JOIN does in SQL.

fields.Front: How is a 1:1 relationship mapped, and which side should receive the foreign key?
fields.Back: Put the primary key of ONE side into the OTHER side's table as a foreign key, along with the relationship's attributes - pick one option, not both. 'It is always better to take the key from the PARTIAL side and put it into the TOTAL side, because then you won't end up with a bunch of null values.' If both are total it does not matter; if both are partial, pick whichever gives fewer nulls.

fields.Front: PROFESSOR (1) Chairs (1) DEPARTMENT: compare the two mapping options.
fields.Back:
Option A - ManageDeptID (FK) in PROFESSOR: Laura NULL, Doug NULL, Michael PS, Stuart MA, Jamie CS, Irving NULL - lots of nulls, because professors do not have to be chairs.
Option B - ManagerID (FK) in DEPARTMENT: MA 18, CS 34, PS 15 - NO nulls, because DEPARTMENT has total participation (every department must have a chair). Option B is correct; the slide's answers use it: PROFESSOR(PK EmpID, FK DeptID), DEPARTMENT(PK DeptID, FK ManagerID).

fields.Front: How does the instructor read the participation lines on Chairs, and how do foreign keys show a relationship between rows?
fields.Back: Single line on the professor side: a professor chairs zero or one departments (partial). Double line on the department side: every department must have a chair (total). A foreign key shows the relationship because its VALUE equals the primary key value of the related row - Laura's DeptID CS links her to the Computer Science row.

fields.Front: Book / Publisher / MovieDeal: map Publishes (1 Publisher : M Book) and Accepts (1 Book : 1 MovieDeal, attribute AcceptDate).
fields.Back:
Publisher (PubID, PubName, Address)
Book (ISBN, Title, Price, Author, Available, PubID (FK))
MovieDeal (Deal_ID, NegotiatorName, StudioName, HeadScreenWriter, ISBN (FK), AcceptDate)
Publishes is 1:M, so the publisher's key goes into BOOK. Accepts is 1:1 and MovieDeal has TOTAL participation, so ISBN goes into MovieDeal (fewer nulls) and AcceptDate travels with it - but AcceptDate is not a foreign key.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: EMPLOYEE (1) --- has --- (N) COMPANY_CAR, and every company car must be assigned to an employee while most employees have none. Which table gets the foreign key, and could you do it the other way?
fields.Back: COMPANY_CAR (the N side) gets EmpID as a foreign key. You could NOT do it the other way: EMPLOYEE would need a list of car IDs in one cell, which breaks first normal form. (Note that the 'which side is total' choice only arises for 1:1 relationships; for 1:N the many side always receives the key.)

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §9.1.1, steps 3-4): what three approaches exist for mapping a binary 1:1 relationship, and what two for a binary 1:N? Which does this course use?
fields.Back:
1:1 - THREE approaches:
1. FOREIGN KEY approach: put the other relation's primary key into one of the two, preferring the TOTAL-participation side. The book calls it 'the most useful' and says it should be followed unless special conditions exist.
2. MERGED RELATION approach: merge both entity types AND the relationship into a SINGLE table. Possible only when BOTH participations are total, because only then do the two tables always hold the same number of rows.
3. CROSS-REFERENCE or RELATIONSHIP RELATION approach: a third table holding both primary keys as foreign keys; one becomes its primary key and the other a unique key. Drawback: an extra table and extra joins.
1:N - TWO approaches:
1. FOREIGN KEY approach, preferred 'as it reduces the number of tables'.
2. RELATIONSHIP RELATION approach, whose primary key is the N-side key alone; worth using only 'if few tuples in S participate in the relationship, to avoid excessive NULL values'.
THIS COURSE USES THE FOREIGN KEY APPROACH FOR BOTH, EVERY TIME.

fields.Text: A 1:N relationship is mapped by putting the {{c1::primary key of the 1 side}} into the {{c1::N-side (many) table}} as a {{c1::foreign key}}, together with any attributes of the relationship.

For 1:N the foreign key goes on the {{c1::N (many)}} side; for 1:1 it goes into the table with {{c1::total participation}}; putting foreign keys in {{c1::both}} tables of a 1:1 is an error, as is naming relationship attributes such as Hours or AcceptDate foreign keys.
A foreign key column does {{c1::not}} need a particular name - 'I call it {{c1::DeptID}}, I could have called it {{c1::WorksInID}}'; on the slide it is marked as a foreign key by a star (asterisk).
